chunks: Describing your RTL experience. The question: Describe any experience you have with RTL.
The interviewer wants to know what you have actually built in RTL (register-transfer level, the code that describes digital hardware), and whether you think like a hardware engineer.
They cannot see your code. So they listen to one real project for your role, your technical choices, and how you checked and measured the result.
Honesty about a small project beats a big claim you cannot explain.
A good answer is a short story with a clear beginning, middle and end.
It names the project and your part, explains one or two design decisions and why you made them, describes how you tested it, and ends with a number and a lesson.
It is like a trip report. A listener should come away knowing exactly what you did, what went wrong, and what you learned.
The loop an interviewer expects you to have gone round at least once.
Mention each stage you really touched; the arrow from timing back to RTL is where most of the learning happens.
RTL: code in Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL that describes registers (storage cells) and the logic (decision circuits) between them.
Synthesis: the tool step that turns RTL into gates (tiny logic circuits). Testbench: simulation code that drives the design's inputs and checks its outputs.
Timing report: the tool's list of the slowest paths and whether they meet the clock.
Inferred latch: an unwanted memory element created when a code branch forgets to assign an output.
Use this skeleton and fill in the [placeholders] with true details.
"I built [a UART transmitter, an SPI controller, a FIFO] in [language] for [class, internship or hobby project] .
My part was [the blocks you wrote] , mainly [a finite state machine plus a counter] .
I tested it with [a self-checking testbench with corner cases] and found [a real bug and its cause] .
Synthesis showed [frequency and size numbers] , and I improved the slowest path by [your fix] ." That is the whole idea.
"My RTL experience is [your project, for example a UART or a small processor] in [language] on [FPGA or ASIC flow] .
I wrote the FSM and datapath with clocked registers and combinational logic, verified it with a self-checking testbench, then ran synthesis and looked at timing and utilization.
The biggest lesson was [a real bug you hit] . I'm comfortable going into any part of it."
Quick check. Which assignment should you normally use for registers in a clocked always block?
